# Preface {.unnumbered}

Medicine has always had two jobs: to treat disease, and to protect health. The second is easy to
neglect, because its effects are gradual and it is rarely an emergency. Yet it offers large gains in
length and quality of life. *Health in Medicine* is about that second job: the everyday
clinical work of helping people stay well. Nutrition is central to that work.

In Singapore, keeping people well now has a national plan. Healthier SG, launched on 5 July 2023 [@mohHSGEnrolment2023]
after its 2022 White Paper to Parliament, set out to re-orient the health system *"from reactively
caring for those who are already sick, to proactively preventing individuals from falling ill"*
[@mohHealthierSG]. Every resident is invited to enrol with a family doctor and build a personalised
health plan around diet, activity, screening and sleep. What people eat, and how they eat, is at the centre
of that plan and is the subject of this book.

## Why a whole book on nutrition

Non-communicable diseases (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancers, chronic respiratory disease)
now cause around three-quarters of deaths worldwide, setting aside deaths from the COVID-19 pandemic
[@whoNCD2025]. They are, in large part,
lifestyle-related diseases, and diet is among the largest modifiable risk factors [@gbd2019diet]. Close
to home, one in three Singaporeans has a lifetime risk of diabetes [@mohWarOnDiabetes]. Diet quality
contributes to that risk: the National Nutrition Survey 2022 found that only about 4% of the staples
residents eat are wholegrain, that nine in ten exceed the sodium target, and that saturated fat makes
up a large share of fat intake [@mohNNS2022].

Diet is one of the main things a doctor can help a patient change, yet it gets little time in
medical training. A 2019 review across five world regions concluded that *"nutrition is
insufficiently incorporated into medical education, regardless of country, setting, or year of
medical education"* [@crowley2019]. In Singapore, by contrast, NUS Medicine has launched a Master of Science in Nutrition and
Lifestyle Medicine, aimed at the challenges of Asia's ageing population and rising chronic disease
[@nusMScNLM].

## What this book is

*Health in Medicine* is an interactive companion to medical-school teaching in nutrition and
metabolism. It starts from Singapore: it is built on tools that are already part of daily
life here, and moves from them to the international evidence. Those tools include My Healthy
Plate's "quarter, quarter, half", Nutri-Grade on *kopi* and bubble tea, and the War on Diabetes.

The book is designed to be used in four steps:

::: {.flow}
1. Read the text
2. Explore the diagrams
3. Self-test with the quizzes
4. Rehearse with the cases
:::

Each chapter has concise text, live diagrams, self-assessment quizzes that give instant feedback,
and branching clinical cases. In the cases you practise advising patients in realistic situations:
choosing a *cai png* lunch, facing a high screening glucose, or feeling tired with heavy periods.
All progress is saved locally in your browser; there is no account and no login. In the AI-patient
cases of the two capstone chapters, what you type is sent to a university-hosted model so that the
patient can reply and your consultation can be given feedback; the book's server does not log message
content.

## How to read it

The book is best read with three habits in mind:

- Read the five parts in order, because the chapters build on each other. The metabolic and
  physiological foundation laid in *Foundations of Nutrition Science* is applied in the four parts
  that follow: *Nutrition across Life Stages*, *Assessing and Advising Patients*, *Nutrition in
  Disease* and *Integrative Cases*.
- Treat the quizzes and cases as the core of each chapter. Counselling is a skill, and skills are
  learned through practice.
- Read every landmark trial together with the caveats that accompany it throughout the book: a
  relative risk on a composite endpoint (several outcomes counted together) is not the same as
  "prevents heart attacks". Learning to read a claim carefully is itself a clinical competency.

## What is covered, and what comes later

This year is about motivation, concepts and the clinical conversation. The aim is to build your
nutritional literacy and your confidence to advise. Prescribing protocols and dietitian training are
outside this year's scope: detailed medical nutrition therapy and disease management come later, and
you will learn *when to refer*.

Helping a patient eat well is a core part of preventive
medicine.
